source_text: Sed quod supra intermisimus, ex parte subsecutae disputationis, ne cohaerentiam ejus dispergeremus, nunc responso expungemus. Ubi enim gradum fiximus de Apostoli absoluta definitione, omnem mulierem etiam omnis aetatis intelligendam, responderi ex diverso habebat, ergo a nativitate et a primo nomine aetatis virginem operiri oportere. Non ita est autem, sed ex quo se intelligere coeperit, et censum naturae suae intrare, et de virginis exire, et pati novum illud quod alterius aetatis est. Nam et principes generis Adam et Eva, quamdiu intellectu carebant, nudi agebant. At ubi de arbore agnitionis gustaverunt, nihil primum senserunt quam erubescendum. Itaque sui quique sexus intellectum tegmine notaverunt. Sed et si propter angelos velanda est, sine dubio ab ea aetate lex velaminis operabitur, a qua potuerunt filiae hominum concupiscentiam sui adducere, et nuptias pati. Ex illo enim virgo desinit, ex quo potest non esse. Et ideo penes Israel illicitum est ad virum tradere, nisi post contestatam sanguine maturitatem: ita ante hunc indicem acerba res est. Igitur si tamdiu virgo, quamdiu acerba est, desinit virginem cum matura cognoscitur, et ut non virgo jam legi applicatur, sicut et nuptiis. Et desponsatae quidem habent exemplum Rebeccae, quae cum ad sponsum ignotum adhuc ignota perduceretur, simul ipsum cognovit esse, quem de longinquo prospexerat, non sustinuit dexterae colluctationem, nec osculi congressionem, nec salutationis communicationem, sed confessa quod senserat, id est spiritu nuptam, negavit virginem velata ibidem. O mulierem jam de Christi disciplina! Ostendit enim etiam nuptias de aspectu et animo fieri, quemadmodum stuprum. Nisi quod etiam Rebeccam quidam adhuc velant. De caeteris vero, id est, quae desponsatae non sunt, viderit parentum procrastinatio ex angustiis vel scrupulositate descendens, viderit et ipsum continentiae votum. Nihil pertinet ad aetatem sua spatia currentem, suaque debita maturitati luentem. Alia in occulto mater, natura, et alius in latenti pater, tempus, filiam suam legibus suis maritarunt. Aspice nuptam jam illam tuam virginem, et animam expectatione, et carnem transfiguratione, cui tu secundum paras maritum. Jam et vox obsolefacta est, et membra completa sunt, et pudor ubique vestitur, et menses tributa dependunt: ac tu mulierem negas, quam muliebria pati dicis! Si congressio viri mulierem facit, non tegantur, nisi post ipsam nuptiarum passionem. Atquin etiam apud ethnicos velatae ad virum ducuntur. Si autem ad desponsationem velantur, quia et corpore et spiritu masculo mixtae sunt per osculum et dexteras, per quae primum resignarunt pudorem spiritus, per commune conscientiae pignus, quo totam condixerunt confusionem, quanto magis tempus illas velabit, sine quo sponsari non possunt, et quo urgente sine sponsalibus virgines desinunt esse! Tempus etiam ethnici observant, ut ex lege naturae jura sua aetatibus reddant. Nam foeminas quidem a duodecim annis, masculum vero a duobus amplius ad negotia mittunt, pubertatem in annis, non sponsalibus aut nuptiis decernentes. Materfamiliae vocatur licet virgo, et paterfamiliae licet investis. A nobis nec naturalia observantur, quasi alius sit Deus naturae quam noster.
pass_a_gloss: But what we omitted above, from the part of the subsequent discussion, so that we would not scatter its coherence, we will now expunge in response. For where we fixed the step concerning the Apostle's absolute definition, that every woman of every age is to be understood, it had to be responded to from the opposite side, therefore from birth and from the first name of age a virgin ought to be covered. But it is not so, but from the point at which she begins to understand herself, and to enter into the census of her nature, and to exit from that of a virgin, and to undergo that new thing which is of another age. For also the first of the human race, Adam and Eve, as long as they lacked understanding, were acting naked. But when they tasted from the tree of knowledge, they first perceived nothing other than that they ought to be ashamed. And so each one of their sex noted their understanding with a covering. But also if on account of angels she is to be veiled, without doubt the law of veiling will operate from that age from which the daughters of men could induce concupiscence of themselves, and undergo marriages. For from that point a virgin ceases, from which she can no longer be. And therefore among the Israelites it is unlawful to hand over to a man, unless after maturity has been attested by blood: thus before this sign the thing is unripe. Therefore if a virgin is such for as long as she is unripe, she ceases to be a virgin when she is recognized as mature, and so that she is no longer subject to the law, just as also to marriages. And those who are betrothed indeed have the example of Rebecca, who when she was being led to her betrothed, still unknown to her, as soon as she recognized him, whom she had seen from afar, did not endure the struggle of the right hand, nor the meeting of a kiss, nor the sharing of a greeting, but having confessed what she had perceived, that is, having been married in spirit, she denied that she was a virgin, unveiled in that place. O woman already of Christ's discipline! For she shows also that marriages are made from sight and mind, just as also stuprum. Unless indeed some still veil Rebecca. But concerning the others, that is, those who are not betrothed, let the procrastination of parents, descending from narrowness or scrupulosity, see to it, and also the very vow of continence. Nothing pertains to the age running its own spaces, and paying its own debts to maturity. Another mother, nature, in secret, and another father, time, in hiding, have married their daughter according to their own laws. Look, your virgin is already married, and her soul in expectation, and her flesh in transfiguration, to whom you are preparing a husband according to the flesh. Already the voice has become obsolete, and the limbs are complete, and shame is clothed everywhere, and the months pay their tribute: and you deny that she is a woman, whom you say suffers womanly things! If the encounter with a man makes a woman, let them not be covered, unless after the very passion of marriage. But indeed even among the gentiles veiled women are led to their husbands. If, however, they are veiled for betrothal, because they are mixed with a male both in body and in spirit through a kiss and right hands, through which they first resigned their shame of spirit, through the common pledge of conscience, by which they agreed to the whole confusion, how much more will time veil them, without which they cannot be betrothed, and by which, when it urges, virgins cease to be! Time is also observed by the gentiles, so that from the law of nature they render their rights to the ages. For they send females to tasks from twelve years, but males from fourteen, deciding puberty in years, not in betrothals or marriages. A virgin is called a mother of a family, and an unmarried man is called a father of a family. Among us, however, natural things are not observed, as if there were another God of nature than ours.

pass_b_english: We left something out earlier, a chunk of the follow‑up argument, so as not to shatter its coherence; now we clear it up in reply. We pinned our case on the Apostle's flat statement that 'every woman' means exactly that — women of every age. The pushback, then, had to run the other way: if the rule applies to all women, a female must be veiled from birth, from the very moment she gets the label 'virgin.' That does not follow. The obligation kicks in when she begins to understand herself, when she enters the census of her own nature, walks out of the category 'virgin,' and undergoes the new thing that belongs to the next stage of life. Adam and Eve, the first of the race, went about naked as long as they lacked understanding. The moment they tasted the tree of knowledge, the very first thing they sensed was that they ought to be ashamed (Gen 2–3). So each sex marked its new awareness with a covering. Even if the stated reason for veiling is 'because of the angels,' the law of the veil unmistakably takes effect at the age when daughters of men can stir concupiscence in themselves and become eligible for marriage (Gen 6:2). From that point a virgin ceases to be a virgin — from the moment she can no longer be one. That is why in Israel it was illegal to hand a girl over to a man until her maturity had been attested by blood; before that sign the thing is unripe. Therefore, if she is a virgin only while she is unripe, she stops being a virgin once she is recognized as mature, and she becomes subject to the law just as she becomes subject to marriage. Betrothed women have the precedent of Rebecca: when she was being led to a husband she had not yet met, the instant she recognized him — the one she had spotted from afar — she did not put up with a hand‑clasp, or a kiss, or an exchange of greetings. She confessed what she had perceived, that she was already married in spirit, and she denied she was still a virgin by unveiling right there (Gen 24). O woman already schooled by Christ! She proves that marriage happens through sight and mind, just as adultery does. Unless, of course, some people still keep Rebecca veiled. As for the rest — those not betrothed — let the parents' foot‑dragging, born of stinginess or scrupulosity, answer for itself, and let the vow of continence answer for itself. Neither has anything to do with the age that is running its own course and paying its own debts to maturity. Another mother, nature, working in secret, and another father, time, lurking in the dark, have married off their daughter by their own laws. Look: your 'virgin' is already married — her soul in expectation, her flesh in transfiguration — and you are busy lining up a flesh‑and‑blood husband for her. Her voice has already deepened, her limbs are fully formed, modesty clothes her everywhere, the monthly cycles pay their tribute: and you deny she is a woman, even while you admit she suffers womanly things! If intercourse with a man makes a woman, then let them not be veiled until after the very consummation of marriage. Yet even among the gentiles veiled women are led to their husbands. If they are veiled at betrothal because they have been mingled with a male in both body and spirit through a kiss and joined right hands — the acts by which they first surrendered the shame of the spirit, through the common pledge of conscience by which they contracted the whole confusion — how much more will time itself veil them, since without time they cannot be betrothed, and when time presses, virgins cease to be virgins! The gentiles, too, watch the clock, so that from the law of nature they render to each age its due. They send girls to work at twelve, boys at fourteen, fixing puberty by years, not by betrothals or weddings. A virgin is called a matron, and an unmarried man a patron. Among us, however, natural realities go unobserved, as if the God of nature were someone other than our own.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text, including the complex conditional and causal structures. Scripture citations (Gen 2-3, Gen 6:2, Gen 24) are correctly added to provide context for the allusions in the Latin. The translation of 'materfamiliae' as 'matron' and 'paterfamiliae' as 'patron' in the context of the gentiles' customs is a valid interpretive choice for the sense of the text.
